It started as a high pitched, fairly quiet, high-pitched squeak in cold weather (i.e. starting and running below 32F or 0C). Appears to come from the drivers side of the engine compartment. The squeak sounds a bit like bearings that needs some grease or a bicycle chain that needs a little of the same. This squeak has started to spread to warmer and warmer temperatures.

I thought alternator (which is stock) and took it to the mechanic, he said it only needed a belt. The shop replaced the alternator belt and the squeak is less noticable/almost gone. However, it has been replaced with a nice screech...a bit like a banshee...sorry, a lot like a belt that is too loose. Once again, the banshee only comes when it is below freezing.

Ideas?

Hey xoitus!

You can always try the highly technical dish soap diagnostic method. Next time you ssupect it'll screech, with the engine off, take some dish soap and rub it on both sides of a 6 inch portion of the accessory belt. Turn the car on, and see if the noise is gone. If it goes away, your belt tensioner and/or belt is to blame! With a new belt, I'd suspect the tensioner is too loose.

You're lucky in that your tensioner is not automatic, but has to be manually set. This means you don't need to shell out your hard earned dough for a new one. In fact, if you bring it back to your mechanic with your complaint, I'd bet he'd tension the belt tighter for free! At least if he's honest, he would.

Thanks so much /u/Adiabatic! I really appreciate the input.

I have a few nagging things on my old vehicles, so I might be back a few times in the near future. :)

If it turns out to not be coming from the belt, use a methanic's stethoscope or a long thin screwdriver to listen to the distributor when the noise is occurring. On older Hondas the distributor shafts were known to begin to sieze up and make squealing noises, especially after cold engine starts.

The council was worried about the sand dunes. They would move in high winds and get sand around the place. The houses are quite low to sea level and there's always a chance a tidal wave could cause flooding and damage. So the council planted grasses to stop the sand dunes movement and 'erosion'. They called it 'revegetation' where there hadn't been any for thousands of years. Slowly after the dunes were locked down the white sands of the beach receded. The surf banks stopped forming and the beach gradually faded. These days the beautiful beach is only a memory replaced by brown sand and a short bit of beach with cliffs of plants edging sharply.
